rationale: A wins because it finds the nastiest real story in the update and does not decorate the holes: "Substack says its top creators split more than $400M last year — and won't say how the split works" is exactly where a competent reporter starts. B is good, but "One writer's case for moving video and podcasts onto Substack under a 10% cut" is a case-study pitch waiting for a protagonist the update never supplied. A's proof gates are sharper; B sometimes treats missing proof as a future errand instead of a reason to downgrade the angle.
gaps_in_A: "Substack has stopped competing with Mailchimp and started competing with YouTube" overstates the competitive shift; the update supports video/feed expansion, not a clean old-category/new-category handoff.
"face a feed that rewards something they didn't sign up to make" assumes the feed rewards video. The proof list catches this later, but the angle text should not smuggle it in first.

"Video hosting is one of the most expensive infrastructure commitments a platform can make" may be true, but it is external context, not in the update. Source it before making it a load-bearing premise.
gaps_in_B: "One writer's case for moving video and podcasts onto Substack under a 10% cut" needs a named creator, a migration, and individual economics. The update supplies none of those, so this is the softest kept angle.
"This is the next chapter of a story the press is already telling" imports a live coverage peg. The fact block says public funding struggles, not that a current funding narrative is already running.
"the moment writers see video in their subscribers' feeds" invents product behavior beyond the supplied TikTok-style feed fact.
"Next step: `meanest-editor`" is the wrong operational handoff. The next move is proof gathering and journalist-fit-check, not another critique pass.
